transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2028-11-06
Start: 15:05 UTC
Duration: ~48 minutes
Attendees: Jamie Ortiz, Priya Menon, Luca Romano (Redwood); Mark Li, Sarah Gomez, Ravi Patel, Emily Tran (Aphelion)

[00:00] Jamie Ortiz: Hey everyone thanks for joining. Quick agenda — we want to run through a focused Optimize walkthrough: batching and prefetch / prefix KV recommendations, walk a cost model tuned to your traffic, and surface any platform constraints. Is that correct from your side?
[00:12] Mark Li (Aphelion): Yep that's right. We're trying to decide whether to start hosted for speed versus commit to dedicated, and how much engineering effort prefetch would need. Our latency SLO is 200ms p95 for 4 token generations, roughly.
[00:24] Jamie: Cool. Priya will run through the console sims and the cost sensitivity matrix; Luca will highlight the rollout options and fallback policies.
[00:35] Priya Menon: Great — first quick question on traffic profile — does Aphelion have session affinity today? How long are sessions on average, and do you see repeated prompts in a session that would benefit from prefix caching?
[00:45] Sarah Gomez: Most sessions are short, like 2–5 turns, but we do have power users with longer threads. Average prompt length is 120 tokens, response target ~320 tokens. We see many repeated product-context lookups at the start of each session.
[00:58] Priya: Ok that helps. Two quick knobs we model: 1) prefix / KV caching — captures expensive up-front context and reduces token throughput; 2) prefetch (lookahead) — proactively populates KV for likely next prefixes. Lookahead improves hit rate but uses egress tokens and compute.
[01:15] Ravi Patel: Important constraint — for compliance we cannot send product PII to third-party managed KV. If we go hosted, data must be encrypted with our KMS and audit logs available.
[01:25] Luca Romano: We support customer-managed KMS and VPC peering for Private deployments; there's an audit log export for Dedicated/Private. Hosted can be configured with envelope encryption and restricted retention. We'll send details.
[01:38] Mark: Also want to flag budget — if savings from prefetch are small vs engineering time, we may skip it.
[01:45] Priya: Totally fair. Let me show a quick sensitivity chart — assume baseline: 1M monthly sessions, mean requests per session 3, avg total tokens per request without cache 440 tokens. Baseline hosted unit cost used: $0.0008 per token (example).
[02:05] Priya: Scenario A: No cache. Cost = tokens * per-token. Scenario B: Prefix cache only, conservative hit-rate 25% for first-turn prefixes, reduces average tokens per request to 360. Scenario C: Prefix + prefetch (lookahead 1) — up front we issue 0.4 extra lookahead requests per session on avg but increase prefix hit-rate to 55%, net token reduction to ~270.
[02:29] Emily Tran: Wait — extra lookahead requests — do these count as billable tokens?
[02:34] Priya: Yes they do. You pay for the tokens consumed by the prefetch request; but if the prefetch succeeds and reduces subsequent generation tokens by larger amounts, you net save.
[02:44] Sarah: Can you show numbers?
[02:46] Priya: Sure — simplified monthly compute token estimates:
- No cache: 1M sessions * 3 requests * 440 tokens = 1.32B tokens -> $1,056,000
- Prefix only (25% hit): average 360 tokens -> 1.08B tokens -> $864,000 (savings ~18%)
- Prefetch (lookahead 1, 55% hit after prefetch): net avg 270 tokens + 0.4 prefetch requests * 80 tokens prefetch cost = additional ~32 tokens per session; effective tokens ~302 -> 906M tokens -> $724,800 (savings ~31% vs baseline)
[03:22] Mark: Those delta numbers are significant. But if prefetch causes tail latency or bursts, we may need dedicated capacity. How does Redwood handle burst capacity?
[03:33] Luca: Redwood Dedicated offers reserved pools with burstable capacity and autoscaling. For hosted, we have soft quotas and regional fallbacks to keep p95 targets under control; we can also route to cheaper model variants if the main model is saturated.
[03:47] Ravi: For on-prem requirements we might be forced to do Private — what's the typical unit cost delta?
[03:53] Jamie: Private typically has platform fee plus infra; per-token compute might be slightly lower depending on hardware choices. We'll put numbers in the spreadsheet.
[04:02] Priya: Back to the prefetch mechanics — prefetch heuristics: session-based lookahead (predict next prefix by n-gram or small classifier), TTLs on KV entries (we used 10–30s in sim), and fallback to prefix-only if KV misses. Prefetch increases cache hit-rate quickly for predictable flows like product lookup or troubleshooting dialogs.
[04:27] Mark: What's typical required storage / memory for KV at our scale? We have ~120k active concurrent sessions at peak.
[04:34] Priya: For a lightweight prefix KV we store compressed KV entries — rough thumb rule: 1.2KB per active session in memory with aggressive eviction; that would be ~144MB per 120k sessions? Wait, math — actually 1.2KB * 120k ~ 144MB yes, plus overhead for indices. For prefix caches with embeddings we recommend offloading to distributed Redis or in-process LRU depending on latency.
[05:01] Sarah: 144MB seems low — are you including longer history? Most of our sessions store 3–4 prefixes.
[05:08] Priya: Right if multi-prefix history stored then multiply accordingly; the number above assumed one compressed prefix. If 3 prefixes average, it's ~432MB. Still modest for Dedicated, but for hosted we can partition across nodes.
[05:20] Jamie: There's an operational point — prefetch increases writes to cache and slightly increases network egress. In many workloads prefetch payback is within weeks because of token savings, but it depends on your session entropy.
[05:33] Emily: How do you measure entropy?
[05:36] Priya: We use session trace analysis — unique-next-token distribution and prefix reuse rate. That's why we asked for 2 weeks sample traces so we can compute observed hit rates and simulate net token delta.
[05:50] Mark: On security: we need SSO + SAML for console, RBAC for API keys, and an audit trail. Can you accomodate that?
[05:58] Luca: Yes — SAML SSO and RBAC are standard; audit exports for token-level events are available in Dedicated and Private. Hosted can do retention-limited logs plus export on request for enterprise.
[06:10] Ravi: Also our legal wants a clause about data residency if we use hosted — we operate EU + NA retail regions.
[06:16] Jamie: We can pin regions and enforce routing by policy. We'll include region routing info in the follow-up.
[06:22] Priya: Quick note about batching: if you have high concurrency, batching reduces per-token compute by increasing kernel utilization. But aggressive batching increases latency. In our sim we modeled batching windows (10ms, 25ms, 50ms) and concurrency targets.
[06:37] Priya: Example: at 10ms max delay, the average effective batch size might be 2–3 on your traffic, giving ~8–12% cost reduction. At 50ms you might see batch sizes 6–8 -> 25–30% cost reduction but added tail latency.
[06:54] Sarah: Our p95 budget is tight at 200ms so 50ms batching looks risky.
[06:59] Priya: Understood. A hybrid approach: keep latency bound (10–15ms batching) and lean more on prefix cache + prefetch to reduce tokens without adding batching delay. That seems aligned with your product goals.
[07:13] Mark: If we do a POC, what's a minimal test to validate?
[07:17] Priya: Minimal POC: 1) ingest 2 weeks of session traces; 2) Redwood runs a cost sim and a prefetch candidate identification; 3) small synthetic traffic run (50–200 RPS) for 24–72 hours to observe hit rates and latencies on Hosted or Dedicated test pool. That will validate both savings and tail effects.
[07:35] Emily: How long to set up the test environment?
[07:38] Jamie: If Hosted, we can standup the sandbox in days; Dedicated test pool typically needs 1–2 weeks for capacity scheduling. Private/on-prem longer due to install.
[07:47] Ravi: One operational question — how does cache invalidation work for user-specific content? We can't reuse certain prefixes across users.
[07:55] Priya: We namespace the KV by tenant/session; sensitive keys are never cached cross-tenant. Prefix caching is most effective for product descriptions or support scaffolding where content is generic.
[08:09] Sarah: Okay. Can we get the cost model with conservative and optimistic hit-rate variants?
[08:13] Jamie: Yes — we'll run low/med/high hit rate scenarios and include engineering effort estimates for prefetch implementation.
[08:20] Mark: Any known gotchas?
[08:22] Priya: A few — prefetchers that are too aggressive can cause extra egress and wasted compute; TTL tuning is crucial; also need to watch KV hot keys which can spike latency. We recommend adaptive TTL and sharded cache to mitigate single-key hotspots.
[08:36] Ravi: For redwood API, is there built-in tracing to map tokens back to requests for cost attribution?
[08:42] Luca: Yes, console exposes per-request token breakdown and trace ID mapping. You can tag requests with correlation IDs. We'll demo that in the POC.
[08:52] Emily: What about competitor lock-in? If we build prefetch heavily, will it be hard to migrate?
[08:57] Jamie: Prefetch logic lives in your app layer; Redwood provides SDKs and console suggestions. Migration mostly involves moving heuristics and cache keys; we can export configs. We avoid proprietary lock-in at the heuristic layer.
[09:12] Mark: Ok let's recap.
[09:14] Jamie: Recap: Redwood to send cost model spreadsheet and console exports; Aphelion to send 2 weeks traces and confirm SSO/KMS constraints; schedule POC scoping call. Also SE to run a quick KV prefetch sim with conservative assumptions.
[09:29] Sarah: Sounds good. Thanks everyone.
[09:32] Jamie: Thanks all — we'll follow up with the spreadsheet and a calendar invite for the scoping session.

End of call.
